newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian markets keep wary eye on Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Asian markets keep wary eye on Wall Street.

text.p: Jittery Asian markets are expected to keep a wary eye this week on Wall Street after plunges on the Dow prompted losses late last week on bourses across Asia.

U.S. stocks tumbled amid fears that the raging bull market may be past its prime and a rise in long-term Treasury yields led the Dow Jones Industrial Average to shed 170 points before it steadied on Friday.
In late trade on Friday, the U.S. index was up 0.77 of a point at 6304.10. But for the week, it was off 217.60 points.

This week sees a Federal Reserve report on November U.S. industrial production, data on capacity use -- the portion of the nation's mines, factories and utilities employed in its production -- and November housing starts.
TOKYO - The Tokyo stock market is likely to focus on regaining stability, after slumping below the 20,000 level for the first time in three months on Friday, brokers said.

"After the benchmark skidded past the 20,000 threshold, the next resistance is pegged at 19,500 to 19,600, which is quite far away," an official at an investment trust affiliated with a "Big Four" brokerage said.
However, some brokers said that pension and public funds are likely to cushion falls, especially below 20,000.
On Friday, the Nikkei 225 ended 159.81 points or 0.78 percent down at 20,341, after tumbling as low as 19,951.69, dented by the Dow's steep fall on Thursday of nearly 100 points.
HONG KONG - Hong Kong stocks are likely to be pressured in part by trends in international equity markets and by an over-extension of values locally, brokers said.
But most remain optimistic on the longer term outlook.
"The secular bull market is not over, but it is overdue for a correction," said Chris Roberts, regional technical analyst at HSBC James Capel. "We could see further declines."
The Hang Seng Index closed down 269.21 points at 12,784.07 on Friday on heavy turnover of HK$10.10 billion.
The index fell 318.66 points or 2.4 percent over the week.
BANGKOK - The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index is expected to rise slightly as investors buy stocks which have been oversold in the past few months, brokers said.
Also, foreign sell orders are expected to decrease as the holiday season approaches, they said.
The SET index closed at a 42-month low of 872.67 on Friday, compared to 876.89 last Friday.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are likely to stay range-bound, with no factors to push the market, brokers said.
"I don't see much movement in the offing," said Mehul Patel, a dealer at brokerage Mukesh Babu Securities Ltd. "Everyone wants to play safe before the year ends."
The top-30 Bombay Stock Exchange index rose 53.85 points, or 1.9 percent, to a provisional 2,880.05 this week.
DHAKA - Traders in the kerb market, nervous about continuing falls in share prices, staged a protest in front of the Dhaka bourse which forced suspension of trading for two sessions.
The downtrend halted after the government ordered the state-owned Investment Corporation of Bangladesh (ICB) to extend support to the market, prompting gains in the last three sessions.
Brokers said although the ICB was behind the rescue, retail investors are also returning. The DSE benchmark index lost 10.5 points to 2,656.6 in the week ending Thursday.
JAKARTA - Brokers and analysts said the market is expected to be mixed, with a possible positive move in certain stocks due to year-end window dressing.
"As usual, many companies are doing year-end window dressing, so its possible the index could be maintained at its current level," Sastra Karta, fund management director of PT Bhakti Investama said.
On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed at 624.46 points, against last week's close 628.12 points.
KARACHI - Pakistani stocks are expected to drift lower on political uncertainty and position-squaring when the market reopens after the Friday-Saturday weekend, dealers said.
A dealer at Ali Husain Rajabali said political jitters had depressed market sentiment.
On Thursday, the Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index closed 0.47 points, or 0.03 percent higher at 1,413.59 compared to a fall of 14.72 points, or 1.0 percent, to 1,460.58 the previous week.
KUALA LUMPUR - Traders foresee a stable to slightly softer week for Malaysian stocks.
The Composite Index fell 2.87 points to 1188.45 on Friday from a week ago. The Second Board was up 4.16 to 545.06.
"The start of the week should see some bargain hunting. It's an opportune time to buy," said Razani Radzi, research manager at P.B. Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
"Every time it (the index) has hit 1,194 it has bounced back down, so it will probably drift lower and stabilise around 1,174," said Tony Shue, a Jupiter Securities institutional dealer.
MANILA - The Philippine stock market is likely to consolidate as it continues to take its cue from U.S, shares, traders said.
"We're expecting sluggish trading and for the market to continue to mirror the Dow's movements," said Allan Tuazon, Urbancorp Securities analyst.
Manila's main index ended on Friday at 3,120.20 points -- 9.25 points, or 0.613 percent lower than the previous week's 3,139.45.
SEOUL - A threatened series of strikes led by the nation's biggest labour union body and a bleak market outlook will keep depressing share prices in Seoul, brokers said.
"It's unlikely for the market to show a major rebound. A sharp fall is even possible if the situation goes worse than we expect now," said Choo Hee-yup of Dongwon Securities.
The composite index closed at 689.07 on Friday, down 1.5 percent or 10.82 points from the previous Friday's 699.89.

SINGAPORE - Dealers in Singapore said the benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index is likely to consolidate at 2,150 to 2,200 till year end and is unlikely to be greatly affected by gyrations in U.S. shares.

"Singapore will move in tandem with Wall Street, but we have our own fundamentals underpinning us. Also, I don't see Wall Street's potential drop to be very drastic. They have gone up on real growth with inflation well-contained," a local dealer said.
On Friday, the benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index was at 2,179.14 against 2,190.39 on December 6.

SYDNEY - Australian shares will depend again on a nervous Wall Street for direction, with no major local economic data or corporate activity due for release in the last full trading week before Christmas.

"If the Dow can stabilise and more particularly if bond rates can stabilise then the market will go up quite strongly next week," said Greg Matthews, executive director of Australian equities at fund manger Mercantile Mutual.
The All Ordinaries index ended the week 2.6 points up at 2316.50.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are seen consolidating on worries over downward corrections on Wall Street and other overseas markets, and expected local oil price increases.

"The long-term (market) outlook is good, but short-term caution is expected on worries over further falls in major overseas markets and likely domestic oil price rises," said Ketty Tu, research manager at Typhone Securities.
On Friday, Taiwan's index ended at 6,825.10 points against 6,806.81 a week earlier. A 6,700-6,900 range is seen in the coming week.
WELLINGTON - New Zealand shares on Friday largely withstood the turmoil on major overseas markets, but brokers said the bourse will struggle to gain if weakness overseas continues.
"It was a mixed picture, but really we are only down 12 points and I think that is a pretty creditable performance," said Don Turkington, Cavill White Securities managing director.
The NZSE-40 Capital Index ended 12.60 points down at 2,349.91, down from 2,360.92 a week earlier.
